trajectory_summary: The call opens warm and stays warm throughout — the customer is self-motivated, technically engaged, and volunteers extensive detail unprompted. The rep collects the required verify items and the bill, validates the customer's enthusiasm about his property, and closes a same-morning-preference booking with a locked day and time. The main drag on the call is time spent waiting through the customer's own tech friction rather than the rep creating any resistance.

observed_outcome.quote: K. Yeah. Let's do that. We'll do Monday at 9AM, and then I'll get everything scheduled through on my end here.
observed_outcome.reasoning: A specific day (Monday) and time (9AM) were explicitly agreed to by both parties, with a stated confirmation text to follow, meeting the bar for a booked outcome rather than tentative.

bill_anchor_audit.bill_quote: I used to have a $300 a month average bill, but in the last six months, it's averaging anywhere I'm paying anywhere from 600 to $1,100 a month for nothing changing.
bill_anchor_audit.flip_quote: That's way too much to power your house, so we can help for sure. The way our program works is it actually replaces the AES bill with a cheaper solar payment. So it's guaranteed savings right off the bat.
bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: Rep acknowledges the bill pain and immediately pivots to the program as the fix, tying it directly to replacing the AES bill with a cheaper solar payment — this is a strategy-level flip even though it doesn't use the sharper utility-grievance detail the customer offered.

interest_reason_audit.reason_quote: But they built a giant solar field two miles south of my house here. And ever since that went online, my electric skyrocketed.
interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never explicitly asks what interested the customer in solar, but the customer volunteers a strong reason unprompted — a utility-scale solar field going online correlating with his bill spike. The rep acknowledges it with sympathy but does not tie it back into the pitch or the appointment framing.

script_coverage.quote: Hey, Glenn. This is Meg. I'm with Ion Solar.
I've got 312 North Miami Street, Quincy, Ohio. Is that right?
Now I'm pulling up the address on Google Maps, and I'm seeing you've got a lot of trees going on.
What electric company are you with, Glenn?
And do you know how much you're paying AES on average?
The only requirement is that you have a credit score above 670. Is that the case for you?
The easiest way to do that, Glenn, is to look at your your electric bill and see how much power you've used.
We'll do Monday at 9AM, and then I'll get everything scheduled through on my end here. I'll send you a confirmation text once we're good to go.

primary_coaching_focus.quote: But they built a giant solar field two miles south of my house here. And ever since that went online, my electric skyrocketed.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The customer handed the rep a vivid, ready-made grievance against the utility. The rep's response was warm but generic ("that's super weird... we can help for sure") instead of explicitly using the customer's own words to frame solar ownership as the fix — the sharpest bill-anchor opportunity on this call was left partially on the table.

key_moments.quote: You guys were testing me on a number, and I'll ask you if it's still a good number.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer references a prior Ion touchpoint verifying a number with him, implying this may be a recycled or repeat-contact lead rather than a cold paid lead. The rep does not probe what that prior test was or when it happened.

key_moments.quote: And then you can see where the the the south facing roof is wide open, including the garage roof is 90% open.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer is proactively describing excellent roof orientation and openness on both the house and a large detached garage — a strong qualification signal beyond what the standard roof_type_age question would surface.

key_moments.quote: But they built a giant solar field two miles south of my house here. And ever since that went online, my electric skyrocketed.
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer hands the rep a ready-made utility-grievance narrative — his bill spiked after a utility-scale solar field went online near him, which he frames with suspicion ("I hate to say this because I'm not trying to be negative"). This is a natural flip point: the rep could reinforce that his own solar would put him back in control instead of paying a utility that profits either way.

key_moments.quote: I'm a disabled vet, and I've had 31 surgeries reconstructing me over the last twenty some years.
key_moments.stewart_read: Rep responds warmly and thanks him for his service, which the customer receives well and keeps talking — this is a partial credit moment, not a full miss, since engagement continued and warmed further.
